claim: Cation-chloride-cotransporters (CCCs) catalyze transport of Cl- with K+ and/or Na+ across cellular membranes.
source: Cation-chloride-cotransporters (CCCs) catalyze transport of Cl- with K+ and/or Na+across cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a fundamental definition of CCC function stated in the abstract, supported by established scientific knowledge about these transporters.

claim: CCCs play roles in cellular volume regulation, neural development and function, audition, regulation of blood pressure, and renal function.
source: CCCs play roles in cellular volume regulation, neural development and function, audition, regulation of blood pressure, and renal function.
evidence: This statement summarizes established physiological roles of CCCs, drawing from scientific consensus.

claim: CCCs are targets of clinically important drugs including loop diuretics.
source: CCCs are targets of clinically important drugs including loop diuretics and their disruption has been implicated in pathophysiology including epilepsy, hearing loss, and the genetic disorders Andermann, Gitelman, and Bartter syndromes.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical knowledge about CCC pharmacology.

claim: Disruption of CCCs has been implicated in pathophysiology including epilepsy, hearing loss, and the genetic disorders Andermann, Gitelman, and Bartter syndromes.
source: CCCs are targets of clinically important drugs including loop diuretics and their disruption has been implicated in pathophysiology including epilepsy, hearing loss, and the genetic disorders Andermann, Gitelman, and Bartter syndromes.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical knowledge about diseases associated with CCC dysfunction.

claim: The structure of Mus musculus K+-Cl- cotransporter (KCC) KCC4 in lipid nanodiscs was determined by cryo-EM.
source: Here we present the structure of a CCC, the Mus musculus K+-Cl- cotransporter (KCC) KCC4, in lipid nanodiscs determined by cryo-EM.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the manuscript, supported by the cryo-EM data presented.

claim: The KCC4 structure was captured in an inside-open conformation.
source: The structure, captured in an inside-open conformation, reveals the architecture of KCCs including an extracellular domain poised to regulate transport activity through an outer gate.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the cryo-EM map showing the conformation of the transporter.

claim: The KCC4 structure reveals an extracellular domain poised to regulate transport activity through an outer gate.
source: The structure, captured in an inside-open conformation, reveals the architecture of KCCs including an extracellular domain poised to regulate transport activity through an outer gate.
evidence: This is based on structural observations and functional inferences from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Binding sites for substrate K+ and Cl- ions were identified in the KCC4 structure.
source: We identify binding sites for substrate K+ and Cl- ions, demonstrate the importance of key coordinating residues for transporter activity, and provide a structural explanation for varied substrate specificity and ion transport ratio among CCCs.
evidence: This is supported by density features in the cryo-EM map and structural analysis.

claim: Key coordinating residues for K+ and Cl- binding are important for KCC4 transporter activity.
source: We identify binding sites for substrate K+ and Cl- ions, demonstrate the importance of key coordinating residues for transporter activity, and provide a structural explanation for varied substrate specificity and ion transport ratio among CCCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments showing reduced activity when coordinating residues are mutated.

claim: CCCs in mammals include the potassium-chloride cotransporters KCC1-4, the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporters NKCC1-2, the sodium-chloride cotransporter NCC, and CCC8-9.
source: CCCs in mammals include the potassium-chloride cotransporters KCC1-4, the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporters NKCC1-2, the sodium-chloride cotransporter NCC, and CCC8-9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Arroyo et al., 2013; Marcoux et al., 2017; Gamba, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the CCC family members.

claim: CCCs were first characterized as modulators of red blood cell volume.
source: First characterized as modulators of red blood cell volume (Dunham et al., 1980; Lauf and Theg, 1980), CCCs are now appreciated to play critical roles in cellular volume regulation, modulation of neuronal excitability, renal function, auditory system function, transepithelial transport, and blood pressure regulation (Marcoux et al., 2017; Gamba, 2005; Singhvi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature on CCC discovery.

claim: CCCs are targets of drugs including the thiazide and loop diuretics hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide, and bumetanide.
source: CCCs are targets of drugs including the thiazide and loop diuretics hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide, and bumetanide and their disruption is associated with congenital hydrocephaly, epilepsy, hearing loss, Andermann syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, and Bartter syndrome (Gamba, 2005; Jin et al., 2019; Kahle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CCC pharmacology.

claim: Disruption of CCCs is associated with congenital hydrocephaly, epilepsy, hearing loss, Andermann syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, and Bartter syndrome.
source: CCCs are targets of drugs including the thiazide and loop diuretics hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide, and bumetanide and their disruption is associated with congenital hydrocephaly, epilepsy, hearing loss, Andermann syndrome, Gitelman syndrome, and Bartter syndrome (Gamba, 2005; Jin et al., 2019; Kahle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on diseases associated with CCC dysfunction.

claim: KCCs are important for K+ and Cl- homeostasis, including in establishing low neuronal cytoplasmic Cl- concentrations critical for inhibitory neurotransmission.
source: KCCs are important for K+ and Cl- homeostasis, including in establishing low neuronal cytoplasmic Cl- concentrations critical for inhibitory neurotransmission, and in volume regulation in many cell types (Marcoux et al., 2017; Bergeron et al., 2003; Mount et al., 1999; Karadsheh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC physiological roles.

claim: Among KCCs, KCC4 is most strongly activated by cell swelling and high internal [Cl-].
source: Among KCCs, KCC4 is most strongly activated by cell swelling and high internal [Cl-] and is uniquely active in acidic external environments (Marcoux et al., 2017; Bergeron et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC4 regulation.

claim: KCC4 is uniquely active in acidic external environments.
source: Among KCCs, KCC4 is most strongly activated by cell swelling and high internal [Cl-] and is uniquely active in acidic external environments (Marcoux et al., 2017; Bergeron et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC4 regulation.

claim: KCC4 is expressed in tissues including the heart, nervous system, kidney, and inner ear.
source: KCC4 is expressed in tissues including the heart, nervous system, kidney, and inner ear and mice lacking KCC4 display progressive deafness and renal tubular acidosis (Marcoux et al., 2017; Mount et al., 1999; Karadsheh et al., 2004; Boettger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC4 expression patterns.

claim: Mice lacking KCC4 display progressive deafness and renal tubular acidosis.
source: KCC4 is expressed in tissues including the heart, nervous system, kidney, and inner ear and mice lacking KCC4 display progressive deafness and renal tubular acidosis (Marcoux et al., 2017; Mount et al., 1999; Karadsheh et al., 2004; Boettger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC4 knockout mouse phenotypes.

claim: Hearing loss in KCC4 knockout mice is due to disrupted K+ recycling by Dieter's cells in the cochlea and hair cell excitotoxicity.
source: Hearing loss in these animals is due to disrupted K+ recycling by Dieter's cells in the cochlea and hair cell excitotoxicity, while renal tubular acidosis is due to impaired Cl- recycling by α-intercalated cells in the kidney distal nephron (Boettger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on the mechanism of hearing loss in KCC4 knockout mice.

claim: Renal tubular acidosis in KCC4 knockout mice is due to impaired Cl- recycling by α-intercalated cells in the kidney distal nephron.
source: Hearing loss in these animals is due to disrupted K+ recycling by Dieter's cells in the cochlea and hair cell excitotoxicity, while renal tubular acidosis is due to impaired Cl- recycling by α-intercalated cells in the kidney distal nephron (Boettger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on the mechanism of renal tubular acidosis in KCC4 knockout mice.

claim: CCCs display varied substrate specificity and transport stoichiometry despite sharing a common amino acid-polyamine-organocation (APC) superfamily fold.
source: CCCs display varied substrate specificity and transport stoichiometry despite sharing a common amino acid-polyamine-organocation (APC) superfamily fold (Payne, 2012; Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Shi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CCC structure and function.

claim: KCCs cotransport K+:Cl- in a 1:1 ratio.
source: KCCs cotransport K+:Cl- in a 1:1 ratio, NKCCs cotransport 1K+:1Na+:2Cl-, and NCCs cotransport 1Na+:1Cl-.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KCC transport stoichiometry.

claim: NKCCs cotransport 1K+:1Na+:2Cl-.
source: KCCs cotransport K+:Cl- in a 1:1 ratio, NKCCs cotransport 1K+:1Na+:2Cl-, and NCCs cotransport 1Na+:1Cl-.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NKCC transport stoichiometry.

claim: NCCs cotransport 1Na+:1Cl-.
source: KCCs cotransport K+:Cl- in a 1:1 ratio, NKCCs cotransport 1K+:1Na+:2Cl-, and NCCs cotransport 1Na+:1Cl-.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NCC transport stoichiometry.

claim: Under typical conditions, transport by KCCs is outwardly directed while transport by NKCCs/NCCs is directed into cells.
source: One consequence of this difference is that under typical conditions (with [K+]in:[K+]out > [Cl-]out:[Cl-]in), transport by KCCs is outwardly directed while transport by NKCCs/NCCs is directed into cells (Marcoux et al., 2017; Gamba, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature and is based on thermodynamic principles given the transport stoichiometries.

claim: CCCs have a C-terminal domain (CTD) important for regulating expression, trafficking, and activity including through phosphorylation or dephosphorylation of CTD sites in response to cell swelling.
source: First, the scaffold is followed by a C-terminal domain (CTD) important for regulating expression, trafficking, and activity including through phosphorylation or dephosphorylation of CTD sites in response to cell swelling (Rinehart et al., 2009; Bergeron et al., 2009; Frenette-Cotton et al., 2017; Melo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CTD function.

claim: CCCs contain a 'long extracellular loop' with predicted disulfide bonds and glycosylation sites that differs in position and structure between CCCs.
source: Second, CCCs contain a 'long extracellular loop' with predicted disulfide bonds and glycosylation sites that differs in position and structure between CCCs; it is formed by the region between TM5-TM6 in KCCs and between TM7-TM8 in NKCCs (Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Hartmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CCC structural features.

claim: The long extracellular loop is formed by the region between TM5-TM6 in KCCs and between TM7-TM8 in NKCCs.
source: Second, CCCs contain a 'long extracellular loop' with predicted disulfide bonds and glycosylation sites that differs in position and structure between CCCs; it is formed by the region between TM5-TM6 in KCCs and between TM7-TM8 in NKCCs (Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Hartmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CCC structural features.

claim: KCCs are present as monomers and dimers in cells.
source: KCCs are present as monomers and dimers in cells and modulation of quaternary state has been implicated in transporter regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KCC oligomeric states.

claim: Modulation of KCC quaternary state has been implicated in transporter regulation.
source: KCCs are present as monomers and dimers in cells and modulation of quaternary state has been implicated in transporter regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KCC regulation.

claim: A shift from monomeric to dimeric KCC2 during development coincides with an increase in its activity that results in chloride extrusion from neurons (the excitatory-to-inhibitory GABA switch).
source: A shift from monomeric to dimeric KCC2 during development coincides with an increase in its activity that results in chloride extrusion from neurons (the excitatory-to-inhibitory GABA switch) (Rivera et al., 1999; Blaesse et al., 2006; Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC2 developmental regulation.

claim: Homodimerization of KCCs is thought to be largely mediated through CTD interactions, as observed in the recent cryo-EM structure of NKCC1.
source: Homodimerization is thought to be largely mediated through CTD interactions, as observed in the recent cryo-EM structure of NKCC1 (Chew et al., 2019), and calpain-mediated proteolysis of the KCC2 CTD is associated with a decrease in transporter activity (Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the NKCC1 structure and represents an inference based on structural similarity.

claim: Calpain-mediated proteolysis of the KCC2 CTD is associated with a decrease in transporter activity.
source: Homodimerization is thought to be largely mediated through CTD interactions, as observed in the recent cryo-EM structure of NKCC1 (Chew et al., 2019), and calpain-mediated proteolysis of the KCC2 CTD is associated with a decrease in transporter activity (Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on KCC2 regulation.

claim: KCCs heterodimerize with other CCCs and interact with other membrane proteins including ion channels.
source: In addition to self-associating, KCCs heterodimerize with other CCCs and interact with other membrane proteins including ion channels (Blaesse et al., 2006; Simard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on KCC protein-protein interactions.

claim: Cells infected with virus encoding KCC4 displayed increased fluorescence over time in the Tl+ uptake assay, consistent with KCC4 activity.
source: Cells infected with virus encoding KCC4, but not cells infected with a virus encoding an anion-selective volume-regulated ion channel SWELL1 (Kern et al., 2019) or uninfected Sf9 cells, displayed increased fluorescence over time consistent with KCC4 activity (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C demonstrating Tl+ uptake in KCC4-expressing cells.

claim: Cells infected with virus encoding SWELL1 or uninfected Sf9 cells did not display increased fluorescence over time in the Tl+ uptake assay.
source: Cells infected with virus encoding KCC4, but not cells infected with a virus encoding an anion-selective volume-regulated ion channel SWELL1 (Kern et al., 2019) or uninfected Sf9 cells, displayed increased fluorescence over time consistent with KCC4 activity (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C serving as negative controls.

claim: No significant difference in activity was observed between N- and C-terminally GFP-tagged mouse KCC4.
source: No significant difference in activity was observed between N- and C-terminally GFP-tagged mouse KCC4 (Figure 1B,C), in contrast to a previous report for KCC2 (Agez et al., 2017), and C-terminally tagged KCC4 was used for subsequent study.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C comparing the two constructs.

claim: KCC4 was reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs formed by the membrane scaffold protein MSP1D1 and a mixture of phospholipids that approximates the composition of major species in neuronal membranes (2:1:1 molar ratio DOPE:POPC:POPS).
source: KCC4 was extracted, purified in detergent, and exchanged into nanodiscs formed by the membrane scaffold protein MSP1D1 and a mixture of phospholipids that approximates the composition of major species in neuronal membranes (2:1:1 molar ratio DOPE:POPC:POPS (2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine:1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine:1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine)) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Ingólfsson et al., 2017; Ritchie et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for nanodisc reconstitution, with citations supporting the lipid composition choice.

claim: KCC4-MSP1D1 particles are similar in size and shape to KCC4 particles in detergent micelles by cryo-EM.
source: KCC4-MSP1D1 particles are similar in size and shape to KCC4 particles in detergent micelles by cryo-EM, but show improved distribution in thin ice which enabled reconstruction to high resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of cryo-EM images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: KCC4-MSP1D1 particles show improved distribution in thin ice compared to KCC4 in detergent, which enabled reconstruction to high resolution.
source: KCC4-MSP1D1 particles are similar in size and shape to KCC4 particles in detergent micelles by cryo-EM, but show improved distribution in thin ice which enabled reconstruction to high resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and the resulting high-resolution reconstruction.

claim: The cryo-EM map of KCC4 in nanodiscs was reconstructed at 3.65 Å overall resolution.
source: The resulting map, at 3.65 Å overall resolution, enabled complete de novo modeling of the transmembrane and extracellular region of KCC4 and includes two partial extracellular glycosylation sites, a bound K+ ion, and a bound Cl- ion (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is the reported resolution of the final cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The cryo-EM map enabled complete de novo modeling of the transmembrane and extracellular region of KCC4.
source: The resulting map, at 3.65 Å overall resolution, enabled complete de novo modeling of the transmembrane and extracellular region of KCC4 and includes two partial extracellular glycosylation sites, a bound K+ ion, and a bound Cl- ion (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This describes the modeling that was possible with the cryo-EM map.

claim: The cryo-EM map includes two partial extracellular glycosylation sites, a bound K+ ion, and a bound Cl- ion.
source: The resulting map, at 3.65 Å overall resolution, enabled complete de novo modeling of the transmembrane and extracellular region of KCC4 and includes two partial extracellular glycosylation sites, a bound K+ ion, and a bound Cl- ion (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This describes features visible in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: KCC4 is monomeric in the nanodisc structure.
source: KCC4 is monomeric in the nanodisc structure.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Density for the N-terminal region and C-terminal domain (CTD) of KCC4 is not observed in the cryo-EM maps.
source: Density for the N-terminal region and C-terminal domain (CTD), which together comprise approximately half the expressed protein mass, is not observed in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The N-terminal region and CTD together comprise approximately half the expressed protein mass of KCC4.
source: Density for the N-terminal region and C-terminal domain (CTD), which together comprise approximately half the expressed protein mass, is not observed in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on the known sequence and molecular weight of KCC4.

claim: The N-terminal region of KCC4 is weakly conserved and variable in length among CCCs.
source: The N-terminal region is weakly conserved, variable in length among CCCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and is likewise unresolved in the structures of NKCC1 or KCC1 (Chew et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal region is unresolved in the structures of NKCC1 or KCC1.
source: The N-terminal region is weakly conserved, variable in length among CCCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and is likewise unresolved in the structures of NKCC1 or KCC1 (Chew et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other CCC structures.

claim: The N-terminal region of KCC4 is presumed to be highly flexible.
source: We presume it is highly flexible in KCC4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The C-terminal domain of KCC4 is well conserved.
source: The C-terminal domain, while similarly unresolved in KCC1 (Liu et al., 2019), is well conserved, has documented roles in regulation, expression, and trafficking (Arroyo et al., 2013; Marcoux et al., 2017; Payne, 2012; Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Rinehart et al., 2009), and mediates homodimerization of NKCC1 and the Archaean CCC (MaCCC) (Chew et al., 2019; Warmuth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis and citations.

claim: The CTD has documented roles in regulation, expression, and trafficking.
source: The C-terminal domain, while similarly unresolved in KCC1 (Liu et al., 2019), is well conserved, has documented roles in regulation, expression, and trafficking (Arroyo et al., 2013; Marcoux et al., 2017; Payne, 2012; Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Rinehart et al., 2009), and mediates homodimerization of NKCC1 and the Archaean CCC (MaCCC) (Chew et al., 2019; Warmuth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CTD function.

claim: The CTD mediates homodimerization of NKCC1 and the Archaean CCC (MaCCC).
source: The C-terminal domain, while similarly unresolved in KCC1 (Liu et al., 2019), is well conserved, has documented roles in regulation, expression, and trafficking (Arroyo et al., 2013; Marcoux et al., 2017; Payne, 2012; Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Rinehart et al., 2009), and mediates homodimerization of NKCC1 and the Archaean CCC (MaCCC) (Chew et al., 2019; Warmuth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structures of NKCC1 and MaCCC.

claim: No evidence of proteolytic cleavage of the N-terminal region or CTD was found in purified KCC4.
source: We found no evidence of proteolytic cleavage of either region.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry and gel analysis of purified protein.

claim: Mass spectrometry of purified KCC4 showed high coverage (47%) and abundance (81% of all KCC4 peptides) for the CTD.
source: Mass spectrometry of purified KCC4 showed high coverage (47%) and abundance (81% of all KCC4 peptides) for the CTD (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: There is a progressive loss of detailed features and decrease in local resolution in TM11 and TM12 that connect the CTD to the core transmembrane region.
source: We observe a progressive loss of detailed features and decrease in local resolution in TM11 and TM12 that connect the CTD to the core transmembrane region (Figure 2—figure supplements 5B and 6).
evidence: This is supported by local resolution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 5B and 6.

claim: Some two-dimensional class averages show a blurred cytoplasmic feature in the position expected for the CTD.
source: Some two-dimensional class averages show a blurred cytoplasmic feature in the position we expect the CTD to emerge (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,D), but attempts to classify distinct conformations of this feature were unsuccessful.
evidence: This is supported by 2D class averages shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,D.

claim: Attempts to classify distinct conformations of the CTD feature in 2D class averages were unsuccessful.
source: Some two-dimensional class averages show a blurred cytoplasmic feature in the position we expect the CTD to emerge (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,D), but attempts to classify distinct conformations of this feature were unsuccessful.
evidence: This describes the outcome of computational classification attempts.

claim: The monomeric structure reported corresponds to full-length mouse KCC4 with flexible and/or disordered terminal regions.
source: We conclude that the monomeric structure reported here corresponds to full-length mouse KCC4 with flexible and/or disordered terminal regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mass spectrometry, gel analysis, and cryo-EM data.

claim: The monomeric structure of KCC4 contrasts with recent homodimeric structures of Danio rerio NKCC1 and H. sapiens KCC1.
source: The monomeric structure of KCC4 contrasts with recent homodimeric structures of Danio rerio NKCC1 (Chew et al., 2019) and H. sapiens KCC1 (Liu et al., 2019), although dimerization of NKCC1 and KCC1 involve completely distinct interfaces (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published structures cited.

claim: Dimerization of NKCC1 and KCC1 involve completely distinct interfaces.
source: The monomeric structure of KCC4 contrasts with recent homodimeric structures of Danio rerio NKCC1 (Chew et al., 2019) and H. sapiens KCC1 (Liu et al., 2019), although dimerization of NKCC1 and KCC1 involve completely distinct interfaces (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The portion of KCC4 in an early-eluting broad peak from a sizing column displays nonspecific aggregation by cryo-EM.
source: (i) The portion of KCC4 in an early-eluting broad peak from a sizing column (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) displays nonspecific aggregation by cryo-EM.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM analysis of the early-eluting peak.

claim: KCC4 is monomeric before and after reconstitution in nanodiscs as assessed by cryo-EM.
source: (ii) KCC4 is monomeric before and after reconstitution in nanodiscs as assessed by cryo-EM (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Cross-linking of purified KCC4 was observed only at high concentrations of crosslinker.
source: (iii) Cross-linking of purified KCC4 was observed only at high concentrations of crosslinker and was reduced when KCC4 was first deglycosylated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), suggesting some cross-linking in glycosylated KCC4 is from intermolecular glycan-glycan or protein-glycan linkages rather than through transmembrane regions or CTDs (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Cross-linking of purified KCC4 was reduced when KCC4 was first deglycosylated.
source: (iii) Cross-linking of purified KCC4 was observed only at high concentrations of crosslinker and was reduced when KCC4 was first deglycosylated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), suggesting some cross-linking in glycosylated KCC4 is from intermolecular glycan-glycan or protein-glycan linkages rather than through transmembrane regions or CTDs (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Some cross-linking in glycosylated KCC4 is from intermolecular glycan-glycan or protein-glycan linkages rather than through transmembrane regions or CTDs.
source: (iii) Cross-linking of purified KCC4 was observed only at high concentrations of crosslinker and was reduced when KCC4 was first deglycosylated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), suggesting some cross-linking in glycosylated KCC4 is from intermolecular glycan-glycan or protein-glycan linkages rather than through transmembrane regions or CTDs (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-linking and deglycosylation experiments.

claim: No substantial differences were observed in the apparent size of KCC4 or KCC1 extracted from different expression host cells or treated with different combinations of detergents.
source: (iv) No substantial differences were observed in the apparent size of KCC4 or KCC1 (assessed by gel filtration) transporters extracted from different expression host cells or treated with different combinations of detergents used in the CCC structure reports to date (Chew et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The KCC1 dimeric interface is mediated predominantly through protein-detergent interactions between TM regions and protein-protein interactions between an extracellular loop.
source: The KCC1 dimeric interface is mediated predominantly through protein-detergent interactions between TM regions and protein-protein interactions between an extracellular loop (Liu et al., 2019; Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on the published KCC1 structure cited.

claim: The extracellular loop involved in KCC1 dimerization is poorly conserved in KCCs.
source: Notably, this loop is poorly conserved in KCCs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In KCC4, the extracellular loop is incompatible with forming a dimer interface without substantial rearrangement due to steric clashes.
source: In KCC4, the loop is incompatible with forming a dimer interface without substantial rearrangement due to steric clashes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A triple mutation designed to disrupt interaction between extracellular loops in KCC4 (S404E, R405E, G407E) has no effect on transport activity.
source: A triple mutation designed to disrupt interaction between extracellular loops in KCC4 (S404E, R405E, G407E) has no effect on transport activity (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Dimerization as observed in the KCC1 structure is not functionally relevant for KCC4.
source: We conclude dimerization as observed in the KCC1 structure (Liu et al., 2019) is not functionally relevant for KCC4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural incompatibility and mutagenesis data.

claim: In NKCC1, dimerization is mediated predominantly through extensive protein-protein interactions in the CTD.
source: In NKCC1, dimerization is mediated predominantly through extensive protein-protein interactions in the CTD (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the published NKCC1 structure cited.

claim: The CTD regions involved in NKCC1 dimerization appear well conserved in KCCs.
source: These regions appear well conserved in KCCs (Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three pairs of mutations designed to disrupt CTD-CTD interactions in KCC4 (L678R, V680R; L670R, A673R; and S780R, L783R) resulted in a similar, but incomplete, reduction in KCC4 activity (by an average of 36, 41, and 44%, respectively).
source: Three pairs of mutations designed to disrupt CTD-CTD interactions in KCC4 (L678R, V680R; L670R, A673R; and S780R, L783R) resulted in a similar, but incomplete, reduction in KCC4 activity (by an average of 36, 41, and 44%, respectively) (Figure 3C,D,F).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The reduction in activity from CTD mutations is comparable to that observed in a truncated KCC4 construct missing the entire C-terminal region (KCC4ΔC, which includes amino acids 1–658).
source: This reduction is comparable to that observed in a truncated KCC4 construct missing the entire C-terminal region (KCC4ΔC, which includes amino acids 1–658) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Monomeric KCC4 is active.
source: These results suggest that monomeric KCC4 is active and that dimerization through the CTDs in a manner analogous to NKCC1 increases transport activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the activity of CTD mutants and truncated KCC4.

claim: Dimerization through the CTDs in a manner analogous to NKCC1 increases KCC4 transport activity.
source: These results suggest that monomeric KCC4 is active and that dimerization through the CTDs in a manner analogous to NKCC1 increases transport activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the partial reduction in activity from CTD mutations.

claim: KCC4 adopts an inward-open conformation.
source: KCC4 adopts an inward-open conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The outer surface of KCC4 is sealed from the extracellular solution.
source: The outer surface of the transporter is sealed from the extracellular solution, while a continuous cavity extends from the center of the transmembrane region to the cytoplasmic side (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A continuous cavity extends from the center of the transmembrane region to the cytoplasmic side in KCC4.
source: The outer surface of the transporter is sealed from the extracellular solution, while a continuous cavity extends from the center of the transmembrane region to the cytoplasmic side (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The transmembrane region of KCC4 consists of twelve helices (TM1-TM12) with TM1-TM5 related to TM6-TM10 through an inverted repeat.
source: The transmembrane region consists of twelve helices (TM1-TM12) with TM1-TM5 related to TM6-TM10 through an inverted repeat.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: TM2 and TM11 in KCC4 are linked by a membrane buried disulfide bond between amino acids C163 (TM2) and C626 (TM11).
source: TM2 and TM11 in KCC4 are linked by a membrane buried disulfide bond between amino acids C163 (TM2) and C626 (TM11) conserved between KCCs, but not other CCCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The disulfide bond between C163 and C626 is conserved between KCCs, but not other CCCs.
source: TM2 and TM11 in KCC4 are linked by a membrane buried disulfide bond between amino acids C163 (TM2) and C626 (TM11) conserved between KCCs, but not other CCCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A prominent feature of KCC4 is a large extracellular domain extending ~35 Å above the membrane.
source: A prominent feature of KCC4 is a large extracellular domain, unique among proteins of known structure, extending ~35 Å above the membrane.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The extracellular domain of KCC4 is unique among proteins of known structure.
source: A prominent feature of KCC4 is a large extracellular domain, unique among proteins of known structure, extending ~35 Å above the membrane.
evidence: This is based on comparison to other known protein structures.

claim: The extracellular domain is formed by EL3 (the long extracellular loop) and EL4, which pack together and cover ~2/3 of the transporter outer surface.
source: It is formed by EL3 (the long extracellular loop; Hartmann et al., 2010) and EL4, which pack together and cover ~2/3 of the transporter outer surface (Figures 2C–D and 4A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figures 2C-D and 4A.

claim: Sequence comparison suggests the extracellular domain is conserved in all KCCs and not found in other CCCs.
source: Sequence comparison suggests it is conserved in all KCCs and not found in other CCCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extracellular domain structure consists of a short three-stranded antiparallel beta sheet (EL4 S1-3), five short helices (EL3 HA-C and EL4 HA,B), and regions without regular secondary structure.
source: The structure consists of a short three-stranded antiparallel beta sheet (EL4 S1-3), five short helices (EL3 HA-C and EL4 HA,B), and regions without regular secondary structure.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The extracellular domain is stabilized by two disulfide bonds (C308-C323 and C343-C352).
source: It is stabilized by two disulfide bonds (C308-C323 and C343-C352) (Hartmann et al., 2010) and decorated with N-linked glycosylation sites (Marcoux et al., 2017; Weng et al., 2013) conserved among KCCs.
evidence: This is based on structural observation and citation to previous work predicting these disulfides.

claim: The extracellular domain is decorated with N-linked glycosylation sites conserved among KCCs.
source: It is stabilized by two disulfide bonds (C308-C323 and C343-C352) (Hartmann et al., 2010) and decorated with N-linked glycosylation sites (Marcoux et al., 2017; Weng et al., 2013) conserved among KCCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on KCC glycosylation.

claim: Non-protein density consistent with glycosylation is present at four previously identified sites (N312, N331, N344, and N360).
source: Non-protein density consistent with glycosylation is present at four previously identified sites (N312, N331, N344, and N360) (Weng et al., 2013) and we model partial carbohydrate chains at the two stronger sites (N312 and N360).
evidence: This is based on density observed in the cryo-EM map and citation to previous work identifying these sites.

claim: Partial carbohydrate chains are modeled at N312 and N360.
source: Non-protein density consistent with glycosylation is present at four previously identified sites (N312, N331, N344, and N360) (Weng et al., 2013) and we model partial carbohydrate chains at the two stronger sites (N312 and N360).
evidence: This is based on density observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The carbohydrate chain at N312 projects from the EH3 S1-S2 loop underneath an extended segment that leads to TM6A.
source: Notably, the carbohydrate chain at N312 projects from the EH3 S1-S2 loop underneath an extended segment that leads to TM6A.
evidence: This is based on structural observation in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The arrangement of the N312 glycosylation may stabilize the extracellular domain and couple it to movements in TM6A.
source: This arrangement may stabilize the extracellular domain and couple it to movements in TM6A, which moves between functional states in other APC transporters (Shi, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2005; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement and comparison to other APC transporters.

claim: TM6A moves between functional states in other APC transporters.
source: This arrangement may stabilize the extracellular domain and couple it to movements in TM6A, which moves between functional states in other APC transporters (Shi, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2005; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on APC transporter mechanisms.

claim: Mutation of N312 to prevent glycosylation (N312Q) severely reduces KCC4 activity (by an average of 84%).
source: Indeed, mutation of this site (N312Q) to prevent glycosylation severely reduces KCC4 activity (by an average of 84%, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The results provide a structural explanation for functional defects associated with non-glycosylated mutants of KCC4.
source: These results provide a structural explanation for functional defects associated with non-glycosylated mutants of KCC4 (Weng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural role of N312 glycosylation and functional data, with citation to previous work.

claim: The position of the extracellular domain suggests its involvement in conformational changes during the KCC transport cycle.
source: The position of the extracellular domain suggests its involvement in conformational changes during the KCC transport cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural position of the extracellular domain.

claim: A segment of the extracellular domain close to the membrane forms a constriction that seals the internal vestibule from the extracellular solution.
source: A segment of the extracellular domain close to the membrane forms a constriction that seals the internal vestibule from the extracellular solution.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The constriction formed by the extracellular domain is likely the extracellular gate based on comparison to other APC transporters.
source: This is likely the extracellular gate based on comparison to other APC transporters (Figure 4A,B; Shi, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to other APC transporter structures.

claim: In KCC4, residues in EL4, TM1, TM3, and TM10 form an electrostatic and hydrophobic interaction network that seals the gate.
source: In KCC4, residues in EL4, TM1, TM3, and TM10 form an electrostatic and hydrophobic interaction network that seals the gate (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: R140 on TM1B extends towards the extracellular solution to interact with D575 on TM10 and E222 on TM3.
source: R140 on TM1B extends towards the extracellular solution to interact with D575 on TM10 and E222 on TM3.
evidence: This is based on structural observation in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The extracellular domain is positioned immediately above the gate through an interaction between K485 on EL4 and D575.
source: The extracellular domain is positioned immediately above through an interaction between K485 on EL4 and D575.
evidence: This is based on structural observation in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The outer portion of TM1B contributes W143 which, together with F486, surrounds K485 as it projects towards TM10.
source: The outer portion of TM1B contributes W143 which, together with F486, surrounds K485 as it projects towards TM10.
evidence: This is based on structural observation in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The extracellular gate in KCC4 is reminiscent of the extracellular gate in LeuT formed by an electrostatic interaction between TM1 and TM10 (R30 and D404) and capped by EL4 through an interaction with TM10 (D401 and A319).
source: This is reminiscent of the extracellular gate in LeuT formed by an electrostatic interaction between TM1 and TM10 (R30 and D404) and capped by EL4 through an interaction with TM10 (D401 and A319) (Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to the LeuT structure supported by citation.

claim: Disruption of the interaction from the extracellular domain (K485D, K485E, and F486A) significantly reduced KCC4 transport activity.
source: Disruption of the interaction from the extracellular domain (K485D, K485E, and F486A) or the TM region (R140E) significantly reduced KCC4 transport activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Disruption of the interaction from the TM region (R140E) significantly reduced KCC4 transport activity.
source: Disruption of the interaction from the extracellular domain (K485D, K485E, and F486A) or the TM region (R140E) significantly reduced KCC4 transport activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The functional effects of gate mutations are likely due to specific disruption of the interaction between the TM region and extracellular domain because a more subtle change (K485A) or mutation of a nearby, but less conformationally restricted, residue (E222R) had no effect on activity.
source: The functional effects of these mutations are likely due to specific disruption of the interaction between the TM region and extracellular domain because a more subtle change (K485A) or mutation of a nearby, but less conformationally restricted, residue (E222R) had no effect on activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of mutations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Opening of the KCC4 extracellular gate likely requires 'unzipping' of the electrostatic network and rotation of EL4 and the extracellular domain away from the surface of the TM region.
source: By analogy to LeuT and other APC transporters, these data suggest opening of the KCC4 extracellular gate likely requires 'unzipping' of the electrostatic network and rotation of EL4 and the extracellular domain away from the surface of the TM region (Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012; Penmatsa and Gouaux, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to LeuT and other APC transporters, supported by citations.

claim: On the intracellular side of KCC4, a hydrophilic cavity is formed by TM1, TM3, TM6, and TM8 that exposes the inside of the transporter to the cytoplasm.
source: On the intracellular side of KCC4, a hydrophilic cavity is formed by TM1, TM3, TM6, and TM8 that exposes the inside of the transporter to the cytoplasm (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3C-E (note: likely refers to Figure 4).

claim: At the top of the intracellular cavity are Cl- and K+ binding sites.
source: At the top of this cavity are Cl- and K+ binding sites.
evidence: This is based on structural observation in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The intracellular cavity forms a bifurcated pathway for ion access to the binding sites.
source: The cavity forms a bifurcated pathway for ion access to these sites, splitting into two routes approximately halfway through the tunnel due to the position of side chains of N439, R440, and R528.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cavity.

claim: Both sides of the bifurcated pathway are open to an essentially equivalent degree.
source: Both sides are open to an essentially equivalent degree (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The only constriction outside of the local area surrounding the ions is formed at the position of N439 (from TM6B), G525, and L529 (from TM8) where the cavity narrows to ~3.6 Å in diameter.
source: The only constriction outside of the local area surrounding the ions is formed at the position of N439 (from TM6B), G525, and L529 (from TM8) where the cavity narrows to ~3.6 Å in diameter, still sufficiently large for passage of K+ and Cl- ions.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements of the cavity.

claim: The constriction at N439, G525, and L529 is still sufficiently large for passage of K+ and Cl- ions.
source: The only constriction outside of the local area surrounding the ions is formed at the position of N439 (from TM6B), G525, and L529 (from TM8) where the cavity narrows to ~3.6 Å in diameter, still sufficiently large for passage of K+ and Cl- ions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured diameter and known sizes of hydrated ions.

claim: Within ~3 Å of each ion, the cavity narrows such that it would require at least partial ion dehydration.
source: Within ~3 Å of each ion, the cavity narrows such that it would require at least partial ion dehydration.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural measurements and knowledge of ion hydration.

claim: The intracellular cavity surface is markedly electropositive.
source: The cavity surface is markedly electropositive (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic surface calculation shown in Figure 4E (note: likely refers to Figure 4F).

claim: From the intracellular solution up to the position of the Cl-, charged and polar side chains, backbone amides, and a helical dipole contribute electropositive character.
source: From the intracellular solution up to the position of the Cl-, charged and polar side chains (from R440, R528, R535, N131, N274, N439, and N521), backbone amides (from IL1), and a helical dipole (from TM6B) contribute electropositive character.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the residues lining the cavity.

claim: The electropositive character of the intracellular cavity may serve to favor accumulation of the less abundant substrate Cl- near its binding site within transporter.
source: Since intracellular Cl- ions are typically present at lower concentrations than K+ ions, this may serve to favor accumulation of the less abundant substrate near its binding site within transporter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrostatic properties and typical intracellular ion concentrations.

claim: Above the Cl- site and around the K+ site, the accessible surface becomes electronegative and would favor cation binding.
source: Above the Cl- site and around the K+ site, the accessible surface becomes electronegative and would favor cation binding.
evidence: This is based on electrostatic surface analysis and represents an inference about function.

claim: The extracellular surface of the transporter outside of the sealed gate is markedly electronegative.
source: The extracellular surface of the transporter outside of the sealed gate is markedly electronegative.
evidence: This is based on electrostatic surface analysis.

claim: The central discontinuities in TM1 and TM6 result in protein backbone carbonyls and amides not involved in regular hydrogen bonding that are utilized in other APC transporters for substrate binding.
source: The central discontinuities in TM1 and TM6 result in protein backbone carbonyls and amides not involved in regular hydrogen bonding that are utilized in other APC transporters for substrate binding (Shi, 2013).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison to other APC transporters, supported by citation.

claim: Two prominent non-protein density features are observed around the central discontinuities in TM1 and TM6.
source: Around this region, we observe two prominent non-protein density features (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is based on observation of density in the cryo-EM map shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: The two prominent non-protein density features are modeled as bound K+ and Cl- ions.
source: Based on structural, functional, and comparative analyses described below, we model these sites as bound K+ and Cl- ions.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis, functional data, and comparison to other structures.

claim: The K+ ion is surrounded by electronegative groups contributed by backbone carbonyls (N131 and I132 in TM1 and P429 and T432 in TM6) and a tyrosine hydroxyl from Y216 in TM3.
source: It is surrounded by electronegative groups contributed by backbone carbonyls (N131 and I132 in TM1 and P429 and T432 in TM6) and a tyrosine hydroxyl from Y216 in TM3.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the K+ binding site.

claim: The distances between electronegative groups and the K+ ion are consistent with K+ binding (2.8–2.9 Å).
source: The distances between electronegative groups and the ion are consistent with K+ binding (2.8–2.9 Å).
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and knowledge of K+ coordination distances.

claim: The electronegative helix dipoles created by TM1A and TM6A may additionally contribute to a favorable electrostatic environment for cation binding.
source: The electronegative helix dipoles created by TM1A and TM6A may additionally contribute to a favorable electrostatic environment for cation binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement of helices.

claim: The coordinating tyrosine Y216 is conserved in all CCC family members that transport K+.
source: The coordinating tyrosine is conserved in all CCC family members that transport K+.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: In NCC, the position corresponding to Y216 is substituted by a histidine, which likely explains its K+-independence.
source: In NCC, the position corresponding to Y216 is substituted by a histidine, which likely explains its K+-independence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Cl- ion is surrounded by electropositive groups from backbone amides (G433 and I434 in TM6) and a tyrosine hydroxyl from Y589 in TM10.
source: It is surrounded by electropositive groups from backbone amides (G433 and I434 in TM6) and a tyrosine hydroxyl from Y589 in TM10.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the Cl- binding site.

claim: The electropositive helix dipoles created by TM1B and TM6B may additionally stabilize anion binding.
source: The electropositive helix dipoles created by TM1B and TM6B may additionally stabilize anion binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement of helices.

claim: The interaction distances and coordination environment of the Cl- site are reminiscent of Cl- sites in CLC transporters.
source: The interaction distances and coordination environment are reminiscent of Cl- sites in CLC transporters (Dutzler et al., 2003) and the coordinating tyrosine is conserved across CCCs.
evidence: This is based on comparison to CLC transporter structures, supported by citation.

claim: The coordinating tyrosine Y589 is conserved across CCCs.
source: The interaction distances and coordination environment are reminiscent of Cl- sites in CLC transporters (Dutzler et al., 2003) and the coordinating tyrosine is conserved across CCCs.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Mutations at the K+ coordinating site Y216 (Y216A, Y216F, Y216H) resulted in a marked loss in transport activity (by an average of 45, 78, 81%, respectively).
source: Mutations at both sites resulted in a marked loss in transport activity in the Tl+-flux assay: K+-coordinating Y216 mutations Y216A, Y216F, Y216H and Cl--coordinating Y589 mutations Y589F and Y589H reduced activity (by an average of 45, 78, 81, 65% and 59%, respectively) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Mutations at the Cl- coordinating site Y589 (Y589F and Y589H) reduced activity (by an average of 65% and 59%, respectively).
source: Mutations at both sites resulted in a marked loss in transport activity in the Tl+-flux assay: K+-coordinating Y216 mutations Y216A, Y216F, Y216H and Cl--coordinating Y589 mutations Y589F and Y589H reduced activity (by an average of 45, 78, 81, 65% and 59%, respectively) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Altering the electrostatic character around the Cl- site with mutations N131A and N131D resulted in comparable transport defects.
source: Altering the electrostatic character around the Cl- site with mutations N131A and N131D resulted in comparable transport defects.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data.

claim: The observed K+ and Cl- sites are critical for KCC4 activity.
source: We conclude the observed K+ and Cl- sites are critical for KCC4 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data showing loss of activity when these sites are disrupted.

claim: The KCC4 K+ and Cl- sites correspond closely to sites for the same ions in NKCC1.
source: The KCC4 K+ and Cl- sites correspond closely to sites for the same ions in NKCC1 (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5B,E.

claim: The proposed Na+ site in NKCC1 is dramatically reorganized in KCC4.
source: However, the proposed Na+ site in NKCC1 is dramatically reorganized in KCC4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In KCC4, TM8 is rotated farther away from TM1 compared to NKCC1.
source: In KCC4, TM8 is rotated farther away from TM1 and two consecutive Na+-coordinating serines in NKCC1 (conserved in all Na+-transporting CCCs) are substituted by glycine and alanine in KCC4 (and in KCC1-3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Two consecutive Na+-coordinating serines in NKCC1 (conserved in all Na+-transporting CCCs) are substituted by glycine and alanine in KCC4 (and in KCC1-3).
source: In KCC4, TM8 is rotated farther away from TM1 and two consecutive Na+-coordinating serines in NKCC1 (conserved in all Na+-transporting CCCs) are substituted by glycine and alanine in KCC4 (and in KCC1-3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The consequence of TM8 rotation and serine substitution is a loss of three of the five Na+-coordinating positions, providing a structural explanation for Na+-independence in KCCs.
source: The consequence is a loss of three of the five Na+-coordinating positions, providing a structural explanation for Na+-independence in KCCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison to NKCC1.

claim: A second Cl- site in NKCCs extracellular to the K+ site is structurally conserved in KCC4.
source: A second Cl- site in NKCCs extracellular to the K+ site is structurally conserved in KCC4 (Figure 5F), but we do not observe evidence for ion occupancy at this site in the structure.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5F.

claim: No evidence for ion occupancy at the second Cl- site is observed in the KCC4 structure.
source: A second Cl- site in NKCCs extracellular to the K+ site is structurally conserved in KCC4 (Figure 5F), but we do not observe evidence for ion occupancy at this site in the structure.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The second Cl- site is occupied in a recent structure of KCC1 in addition to the K+ and Cl- sites observed in KCC4.
source: Interestingly, this site is occupied in a recent structure of KCC1 in addition to the K+ and Cl- sites observed in KCC4 (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison to the published KCC1 structure cited.

claim: Mutagenesis of Y466 (Y466A and Y466H) near the second Cl- site reduces activity of KCC4, suggesting that the integrity of both sites is important for transport.
source: Mutagenesis of a nearby tyrosine Y466A and Y466H reduce activity of KCC4, suggesting that the integrity of both sites is important for transport (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 5G and represents an inference about the importance of the second site.

claim: The structural and mutational data are consistent with prior evidence for monomeric KCCs in cells in addition to homodimers and other heterooligomers.
source: Our structural and mutational data are consistent with prior evidence for monomeric KCCs in cells in addition to homodimers and other heterooligomers (Blaesse et al., 2006; Puskarjov et al., 2012; Watanabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Comparison of residues in KCC4 that correspond to those in the KCC1 homodimerization interface suggest this interaction is not relevant for KCC4 function.
source: Comparison of residues in KCC4 that correspond to those in the KCC1 homodimerization interface (Liu et al., 2019) suggest this interaction is not relevant for KCC4 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison and mutagenesis data.

claim: Comparison to the NKCC1 homodimerization interface suggest KCC4 could similarly self-interact and mutational data suggests this interaction increases KCC4 activity.
source: However, comparison to the NKCC1 homodimerization interface (Chew et al., 2019) suggest KCC4 could similarly self-interact and mutational data suggests this interaction increases KCC4 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison and mutagenesis data.

claim: If monomeric and dimeric KCC4 are functionally distinct, regulated oligomerization in cells would be an opportunity to modulate transport activity.
source: If monomeric and dimeric KCC4 are functionally distinct, regulated oligomerization in cells would be an opportunity to modulate transport activity.
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Dimerization involving a close juxtaposition of CTDs and transmembrane regions could enable regulation of transporter activity through CTD posttranslational modifications that may not be possible in monomeric KCC4 with a flexibly attached CTD.
source: In addition to an increase in basal activity, dimerization involving a close juxtaposition of CTDs and transmembrane regions could enable regulation of transporter activity through CTD posttranslational modifications that may not be possible in monomeric KCC4 with a flexibly attached CTD (Hartmann and Nothwang, 2014; Blaesse et al., 2006; Puskarjov et al., 2012; Watanabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: A monomeric to dimeric transition in KCC2 has been correlated with an increase in transporter activity.
source: In support of the in vivo relevance of this regulatory mode, a monomeric to dimeric transition in KCC2 has been correlated with an increase in transporter activity (Blaesse et al., 2006) and is influenced by phosphorylation of the CTD (Watanabe et al., 2009), while proteolytic cleavage of the KCC2 CTD correlates with a decrease in activity (Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on KCC2 regulation.

claim: The monomeric to dimeric transition in KCC2 is influenced by phosphorylation of the CTD.
source: In support of the in vivo relevance of this regulatory mode, a monomeric to dimeric transition in KCC2 has been correlated with an increase in transporter activity (Blaesse et al., 2006) and is influenced by phosphorylation of the CTD (Watanabe et al., 2009), while proteolytic cleavage of the KCC2 CTD correlates with a decrease in activity (Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on KCC2 regulation.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of the KCC2 CTD correlates with a decrease in activity.
source: In support of the in vivo relevance of this regulatory mode, a monomeric to dimeric transition in KCC2 has been correlated with an increase in transporter activity (Blaesse et al., 2006) and is influenced by phosphorylation of the CTD (Watanabe et al., 2009), while proteolytic cleavage of the KCC2 CTD correlates with a decrease in activity (Puskarjov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on KCC2 regulation.

claim: The ability of KCC4 to hetero-oligomerize with CCCs and other membrane proteins may be associated with weaker self-interaction compared to other CCCs.
source: The ability of KCC4 to hetero-oligomerize with CCCs and other membrane proteins may be associated with weaker self-interaction compared to other CCCs (Simard et al., 2007; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Goutierre et al., 2019; Ivakine et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed monomeric structure and citations to literature on KCC hetero-oligomerization.

claim: The structure of KCC4 provides insight into the architecture of KCCs and the mechanistic basis for coupled K+:Cl- transport.
source: The structure of KCC4 provides insight into the architecture of KCCs and the mechanistic basis for coupled K+:Cl- transport.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claim: KCC4 is observed in an inward-open conformation that exposes the inside of the transporter to the cytoplasm through a wide and electropositive tunnel that may serve to concentrate the less abundant intracellular substrate Cl-.
source: KCC4 is observed in an inward-open conformation that exposes the inside of the transporter to the cytoplasm through a wide and electropositive tunnel that may serve to concentrate the less abundant intracellular substrate Cl-.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and represents an inference about function.

claim: The inward-open conformation observed in KCC4 is similar to that observed in NKCC1 and KCC1.
source: This conformation is similar to that observed in NKCC1 and KCC1 and presumably represents the lowest energy state for CCCs in symmetrical salt concentrations and the absence of a transmembrane electrical gradient (Chew et al., 2019; Chi, 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison to other CCC structures cited.

claim: The inward-open conformation presumably represents the lowest energy state for CCCs in symmetrical salt concentrations and the absence of a transmembrane electrical gradient.
source: This conformation is similar to that observed in NKCC1 and KCC1 and presumably represents the lowest energy state for CCCs in symmetrical salt concentrations and the absence of a transmembrane electrical gradient (Chew et al., 2019; Chi, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental conditions and comparison to other structures.

claim: K+ and Cl- ions are identified around central discontinuities in TM1 and TM6.
source: We identify K+ and Cl- ions around central discontinuities in TM1 and TM6.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM map.

claim: A Na+ site in the 1:1:2 Na+:K+:Cl- cotransporter NKCC1 is reorganized in KCC4 due to TM-TM displacement and loss of specific coordinating side chains, explaining Na+-independence in KCCs.
source: A Na+ site in the 1:1:2 Na+:K+:Cl- cotransporter NKCC1 is reorganized in KCC4 due to TM-TM displacement and loss of specific coordinating side chains, explaining Na+-independence in KCCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison to NKCC1.
